column1: # The gates CI runs that the measured set does NOT hold, and why.
# COLUMN 1: the gate's name. A python gate is the script's file name; a
#           compiled gate is the subcommand of the binary; a shell gate is
# COLUMN 2: the reason it is out. A reason is not a wish: "we did not get
#           round to it" is not a reason, and the gate
#           `harbor-gates check-gate-bench-set` fails on a row whose reason
# The set of measured gates is bench/gates/tools.tsv. A gate CI runs is
# either in that file or in this one, and the gate that checks this says so
# Three reasons a gate is out, and only three:
#   1. it needs the .NET SDK, and the measuring machine has none;
#   2. it needs the network, and the measuring machine has none;
#   3. CI runs it only as its own self-test, so there is no run of the gate
# The README says the same thing in prose, and the gate checks that every
# name here is named there too: a reason that lives only in a data file is a

column2: CI runs only its own self-test: the assembler is a release-time tool, and a pull request owns its own fragment
the gate downloads the jscpd binary from the network on first use, and there is no network and no binary on the measuring machine
the control runs the compiler: it builds a throwaway project and reads its output, and the measuring machine has no .NET SDK
the demo is recorded by running Harbor and the gate compares two recordings of it, so it needs the built product and the .NET SDK
the workload publishes the CLI with NativeAOT and runs it, so it needs the .NET SDK
the instrument runs `dotnet build` and meters it, so it needs the .NET SDK; the numbers it produces live in docs/BENCHMARKS.md §6

the proof builds a throwaway project against the public-API analyzer and requires it to fail, so it needs the .NET SDK
the runner starts one `dotnet exec` per shard, so it needs the built product and the .NET SDK
